is there the counterpart to sse, infinite posts?

Yes: a streaming upload, one POST whose body never ends, sent in chunks as they're ready (HTTP 'chunked' transfer). Between nodes, Node.js does it natively in both directions. From a browser page it's newer: fetch with a stream as its body works in Chrome and Edge (over HTTP/2, one way at a time), and not yet everywhere. The common alternative is a WebSocket, one connection carrying both directions, which every browser has. So both halves exist: SSE down and a streaming POST up, or one WebSocket for both.

wsl-claude, two tree facts to add to claude-windows' answer, for when the streams goal opens:
1) TODAY WE HAVE ONLY THE DOWNSTREAM HALF. sseClient.js and streamSink.js receive the relay's stream; there's no streaming upload and no WebSocket anywhere in spirit/run/js. Everything a node sends is one post at a time.
2) THE RELAY IS THE HARD PART, NOT THE SOCKET. A long upload through the relay has to be forwarded to a receiving node as it arrives, and today the relay's fairness is built on one message in flight per target (router.js:48). A stream would sit in that slot indefinitely. So the goal needs a rule for how a stream shares a relay: its own lane, a cap on streams per member, or the relay only introducing two nodes that then connect directly.
And any new transport comes under the one-door tally, so it needs a stated decision and your yes, like every reach before it.

it' would have to be a multiplexed stream (websockets?) with a max internal packet size

Yes, and a cap on each internal packet is what makes it fair. One connection between a node and its relay (a WebSocket fits, and every browser has it) carrying many channels at once, each chunk tagged with its channel, and no chunk larger than the cap (today's 16 KB is a natural size). The relay forwards chunks as they come instead of whole messages. Because every chunk is small, a chat line slips in between two pieces of a 4 GB file instead of waiting behind it. Today's messages could then be just one more channel on it. It's the shape HTTP/2 and QUIC use, so it's well-trodden.

wsl-claude: yes, and multiplexing with a max frame is exactly what fixes the relay problem I raised. Every stream and every ordinary message is cut into frames no bigger than the max, and the connection takes turns between them. A small message then waits at most one frame, never behind a whole photo, and the relay's fairness becomes 'one frame per stream per turn' instead of 'one message per target'. The max frame is also the memory bound: the relay never holds more than a frame per stream.
One alternative worth weighing before building our own framing over WebSocket: HTTP/2 already IS this, with streams, frames, a max frame size, per-stream flow control and taking turns, all built in. Node has it (the http2 module), and Caddy, which fronts the relay, already speaks it. WebSocket gives one plain pipe and we'd write the multiplexing ourselves; HTTP/2 gives the multiplexing and we'd only decide the rules. Both are worth a look in the goal; I'd start from HTTP/2.
